Without the NLS, it cannot undergo receptor-mediated nuclear import. Because it is larger than about 40 kDa, it also cannot diffuse passively through nuclear pores. The protein was made on free ribosomes and lacks an ER signal sequence, so it does not enter the secretory pathway; absence of an NLS also does not automatically mark it for proteasomal degradation. Therefore, the mutant protein most likely remains in the cytoplasm and cannot reach its nuclear target genes.

object.final_answer: Iron-bound transferrin will remain in the blood at high levels because developing red blood cells cannot specifically bind and internalize it.
object.working: The mutation prevents transferrin receptors from reaching the cell surface of developing red blood cells. Under normal conditions, these receptors bind iron-bound transferrin in the blood to internalize it via receptor-mediated endocytosis. Without receptors on the cell surface, these cells cannot bind or internalize the iron-bound transferrin. Consequently, the iron-bound transferrin cannot enter the cells and will remain in the bloodstream at abnormally high levels. This directly supports choice C.
